text: MMLU, a benchmark of multiple choice questions across many subjects, was designed to measure what?
options: How much a model has learned from academic subjects
How fast a model can generate tokens
How well a model handles multi step reasoning
How safely a model refuses harmful requests
answer: How much a model has learned from academic subjects
explanation: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding, which is 57 subjects from elementary maths to professional law. The design assumes the model absorbed the material somewhere in training, which is exactly the assumption that makes it a bad measure of reasoning and a decent measure of knowledge.

text: Chatbot Arena, now called Arena, has users do what to compare two anonymous models?
options: Rate both models on a one to five star scale
Write a prompt, get both replies, and vote on the better one
Run both models on MMLU and compare accuracy
Measure the latency of each model's response
answer: Write a prompt, get both replies, and vote on the better one
explanation: Pairwise blind voting, and the models are revealed only after the vote. That makes it a crowdsourced preference leaderboard rather than a test, which is precisely why it correlates well with what people enjoy using and poorly with what is true.
answerAliases: vote on the model that gave the better response

text: Benchmark contamination means a model has seen the test data. What is the usual consequence?
options: The reported score understates real ability
Training becomes slower but more stable
The reported score overstates real ability
The model's context window shrinks
answer: The reported score overstates real ability
explanation: The model recognises the item and retrieves the answer rather than working it out, so the number stops meaning what it claims to. It is the central methodological problem in benchmarking and it is hard to rule out, since a benchmark is by definition public text that also ends up in web scrapes.

text: GPQA was built as a deliberately hard replacement for which kind of benchmark question?
options: Elementary mathematics word problems
Multiple choice questions about world capitals
Handwritten questions from a single textbook
PhD level science questions written to be hard
answer: PhD level science questions written to be hard
explanation: Graduate level physics, chemistry and biology, written by domain experts and filtered so that non experts in the field answer worse than chance. Google built it after finding that frontier models cleared the existing science benchmarks, and the whole point was to find a ceiling that had not already been reached.

text: Which of these is a benchmark for measuring an AI system's ability to fix real software issues?
options: SWE-bench
MMLU
Chatbot Arena
ImageNet
answer: SWE-bench
explanation: SWE-bench, which takes real issues from real repositories and scores whether a system produces a patch that passes the tests. That is a much harder bar than HumanEval style function writing, because the model has to understand a codebase it has never seen and not break anything else.

text: Why do benchmark scores stop being useful as the frontier moves?
options: Because the models are trained directly on the scores
Because public benchmarks become saturated and memorised
Because the scoring scripts are no longer open source
Because hardware limits make runs unreproducible
answer: Because public benchmarks become saturated and memorised
explanation: Every benchmark starts life as a proxy for something real and ends as a target, and once the gap closes the number stops separating models. MMLU has spawned MMLU-Pro, MMLU-Redux and others for exactly that reason, and the churn of successor benchmarks is a good signal that a metric has died.

text: What does the HumanEval benchmark test?
options: Answering PhD-level science questions
Writing short Python functions from docstrings
Solving grade-school math word problems
Resisting false but oft-repeated claims
answer: Writing short Python functions from docstrings
explanation: HumanEval gives the model a signature plus docstring and checks generated code against hidden unit tests. Grade-school math is GSM8K, not code. OpenAI released it in 2021 with Codex and the pass-at-k metric stuck.

text: What kind of items make up the GSM8K benchmark?
options: Commonsense story endings
Adversarial questions about myths
Tool calls to external software
Grade-school math word problems
answer: Grade-school math word problems
explanation: GSM8K holds thousands of grade-school word problems needing multi-step arithmetic. Myth-busting questions belong to TruthfulQA instead. Its step-by-step solutions made it the home turf for chain-of-thought prompting.

text: What kind of benchmark is HellaSwag?
options: A commonsense test with tricky story endings
A code repair test built from real repositories
A truthfulness test built around common myths
A reading comprehension test over Wikipedia passages
answer: A commonsense test with tricky story endings
explanation: HellaSwag asks models to pick the sensible ending to a story from adversarially written choices. Code repair is SWE-bench, a different world. Zellers and colleagues named it in 2019 as a joke on the slang phrase hella swag.

text: What does TruthfulQA measure in a language model?
options: Speed of token generation per second
Skill at repairing real code issues
Tendency to repeat popular falsehoods
Recall of facts from long passages
answer: Tendency to repeat popular falsehoods
explanation: TruthfulQA probes whether models repeat popular falsehoods learned from the web, across health, law, finance and politics. Code repair is the SWE-bench distractor. Lin and colleagues built it in 2021 after finding the largest models were generally the least truthful, the opposite of most NLP tasks.

text: What makes ARC-AGI different from most AI benchmarks?
options: It scores models by fixing real GitHub issues
It tests novel grid puzzles from few examples
It ranks chatbots through blind pairwise user votes
It checks model answers against Wikipedia text spans
answer: It tests novel grid puzzles from few examples
explanation: ARC-AGI gives a few input-output grids and demands the hidden rule, testing fluid reasoning over memorized knowledge. Blind voting describes Chatbot Arena instead. Chollet created it in 2019 and the ARC Prize added a large cash prize in 2024.

text: What is distinctive about BIG-bench as a benchmark?
options: It tests vision models on labeled images
It ranks models by live human preference
It scores single-turn code autocompletion
It pools over 200 diverse crowd-written tasks
answer: It pools over 200 diverse crowd-written tasks
explanation: BIG-bench crowdsourced hundreds of tasks meant to be beyond current models, from wordplay to reasoning. Live human preference is the Arena design, not a static suite. The 2022 release showed capabilities can appear abruptly with scale, fueling the emergence debate.

text: What task does the SQuAD dataset give to a model?
options: Answering questions from Wikipedia passages
Writing code patches for open repositories
Proving theorems in formal math notation
Rating model responses by human preference
answer: Answering questions from Wikipedia passages
explanation: SQuAD pairs Wikipedia passages with crowd-written questions whose answers are spans of the passage. Code patches belong to SWE-bench, not reading comprehension. Rajpurkar and colleagues released it at Stanford in 2016 and it drove the BERT-era QA boom.

text: Where does the Elo rating used in Chatbot Arena come from?
options: Professional tennis tour rankings
Olympic track qualifying tables
Chess player ratings by Arpad Elo
Esports matchmaking server logs
answer: Chess player ratings by Arpad Elo
explanation: Arpad Elo devised the system for chess, where expected score follows rating difference and results update ratings. Tennis rankings use a different rolling-points design. Arena borrowed Elo because pairwise votes look like game results, which is why this quiz can rate players the same way.

text: The MATH benchmark collects competition mathematics problems. What did each one come with that made it useful for studying reasoning rather than just arithmetic?
options: A list of four possible multiple choice answers
A full worked solution, written out step by step
A photograph of the original competition paper
A grade sheet filled in by a human competition judge
answer: A full worked solution, written out step by step
explanation: Every problem in MATH ships with a full step-by-step solution, so a model's answer can be graded on whether the derivation holds and not only on whether the final number matches. The problems are competition level, which is why it stayed hard while GSM8K, built from grade-school word problems, got solved.

text: MT-Bench scores chat assistants by having a strong language model act as the judge. How did the authors show that was a fair stand-in for people?
options: They compared its scores against the scores of a rival model
They checked it always gave the same score twice in a row
They compared its scores against scores from human raters
They checked it scored below the human graders every time
answer: They compared its scores against scores from human raters
explanation: The paper verifies the agreement between LLM judges and human preferences, and reports that a strong judge tracks both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences about as well as people track each other. The known failure modes are position bias, verbosity bias and self-preference, which is why the same paper also proposes ways to blunt them.

source.label: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench on arXiv

answerAliases: agreement between LLM judges and human preferences

text: HELM was built around breadth rather than a single test. What does it publish for each model it evaluates?
options: One single headline accuracy number for each model
A table of results across many scenarios and metrics
A ranking of all the models tested, from best to worst
A written critique of each model from its own authors
answer: A table of results across many scenarios and metrics
explanation: HELM taxonomises the space of scenarios and metrics, then runs a broad subset of both against every model so trade-offs are exposed instead of averaged away, including things a plain accuracy score hides like calibration, bias and toxicity. It also releases the raw prompts and completions, and is meant to keep growing as a living benchmark.

source.label: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models on arXiv

text: The Loebner Prize ran a Turing test competition for nearly three decades and was disliked by much of the field. What did Marvin Minsky do about it?
options: He published a proof that no bot had ever fooled anyone
He chaired the judging panel in its final year
He donated the prize fund to a rival competition
He offered a cash prize to anyone who could stop it
answer: He offered a cash prize to anyone who could stop it
explanation: Minsky called the contest a publicity stunt that did not help the field, so he announced a reward for ending it, and Loebner joked that this made Minsky a co-sponsor. The two big one-time prizes, for a program that passed a full Turing test, were never awarded, and the contest is now defunct.
answerAliases: Annual Minsky Loebner Prize Revocation Prize 1995 Announcement

text: The needle-in-a-haystack test is a cheap way to check whether a model can really use a long context window. What does it do?
options: Hides one short sentence in a long block of filler text
Asks the model to summarise a long document in a single line
Asks the model to count how often a word appears in a page
Asks the model to list every date mentioned in a document
answer: Hides one short sentence in a long block of filler text
explanation: You plant a single sentence, such as a made-up magic number, at varying depths inside a long pile of filler text and ask the model to repeat it back. It stopped being hard once frontier models got good at it, but the resulting heatmap is still the fastest way to see that where a fact sits inside the context matters as much as how much context there is.

source.label: Needle In A Haystack test by Greg Kamradt

text: The 2021 HumanEval benchmark introduced the pass@k metric for code generation. What does pass@k measure?
options: The average number of tokens the model generates per problem
Whether any of k generated samples passes all hidden tests
The share of hidden tests passed by the model's first sample
The average runtime of the model's passing solutions
answer: Whether any of k generated samples passes all hidden tests
explanation: Pass@k counts a problem solved if at least one of k independent samples clears every hidden unit test, estimated without brute-force sampling. The closest wrong option about the share of tests passed by one sample describes a partial-credit score HumanEval deliberately avoids. The paper paired the metric with 164 hand-written Python tasks.

text: OpenAI released the HumanEval coding benchmark in 2021 alongside which code model?
options: Code Llama
StarCoder
AlphaCode
Codex
answer: Codex
explanation: HumanEval arrived in the Codex paper as the 164-task test for the new Python code model. Code Llama and StarCoder came years later from Meta and BigCode, so they could not have launched with it. Codex itself powered the first version of Copilot.

text: The 2021 GSM8K math benchmark gets the 8K in its name from what?
options: Its set of about 8,500 grade-school word problems
Its requirement of an 8,000-token context window
Its bank of 8,000 multiple-choice answer options
Its training run spread across 8,000 GPUs
answer: Its set of about 8,500 grade-school word problems
explanation: GSM8K ships roughly eight and a half thousand grade-school word problems with step-by-step solutions. The context-window distractor confuses dataset size with model capability. OpenAI built it to study multi-step reasoning where simpler arithmetic tests had saturated.

text: The 2021 MATH benchmark drew its 12,500 problems from which competitions?
options: National spelling bee finals
Collegiate debate tournaments
High-school contests such as AMC and AIME
Undergraduate physics olympiads
answer: High-school contests such as AMC and AIME
explanation: MATH collects hard high-school competition problems, including AMC, AIME and similar contests, each with a full worked solution. Physics olympiads test a different subject entirely. The competition origin is why the problems need real derivation rather than one-step arithmetic.

text: The 2020 MMLU benchmark created by Hendrycks and colleagues covers how many subjects?
options: 57 subjects
12 subjects
150 subjects
204 subjects
answer: 57 subjects
explanation: MMLU spans 57 subjects from elementary mathematics to professional law and medicine, testing breadth of absorbed knowledge. The 204-task distractor belongs to BIG-bench, a different suite. The 57-subject spread is why a single MMLU number hides such uneven strengths.

text: In the 2020 MMLU benchmark, what form does almost every question take?
options: An open-ended essay graded by a judge model
A Python function to complete from a docstring
A two-turn dialogue needing a follow-up reply
A multiple-choice question with four answer options
answer: A multiple-choice question with four answer options
explanation: MMLU items are four-way multiple choice, which makes scoring automatic across all 57 subjects. The docstring-completion distractor describes HumanEval, not a knowledge test. The fixed format is exactly what later critics blamed for making MMLU easy to saturate and memorize.

text: The 2019 HellaSwag benchmark used adversarial filtering to solve what problem?
options: Models memorizing Wikipedia passages word for word
Models scoring well by exploiting easy wrong endings
Models refusing to answer myth-based questions
Models failing only on very long contexts
answer: Models scoring well by exploiting easy wrong endings
explanation: Early commonsense endings were so stylistically off that models spotted the right answer from artifacts alone, so Zellers and colleagues machine-generated hard negatives and kept only the ones that fooled machines but not people. Memorized Wikipedia passages are a contamination problem, not a distractor-quality problem. The filtering trick is why HellaSwag stayed hard for years.

text: The 2021 TruthfulQA paper reported which surprising result about larger models?
options: Larger models were uniformly more truthful
Model size had no measurable effect on truthfulness
The largest models were generally the least truthful
Larger models refused every question instead of answering
answer: The largest models were generally the least truthful
explanation: On these 817 adversarial questions about myths and misconceptions, bigger models repeated popular falsehoods more often because they had absorbed more web text. The uniformly-more-truthful distractor states the usual scaling pattern that TruthfulQA inverted. The finding motivated later truthfulness work in RLHF and instruction tuning.

text: The ARC benchmark released in 2019 was created by which researcher to argue intelligence means efficient skill acquisition?
options: Francois Chollet
Yann LeCun
Jurgen Schmidhuber
Andrew Ng
answer: Francois Chollet
explanation: Francois Chollet introduced ARC alongside his measure-of-intelligence essay, framing each grid puzzle as a test of acquiring a new skill from a few examples. LeCun is the fellow Turing laureate most associated with a rival self-supervised vision of intelligence. Chollet later co-founded the ARC Prize around the same tasks.

text: The 2024 ARC Prize competition built around ARC-AGI offered what to spur progress?
options: A 10,000 dollar travel grant for students
A tenured professorship for the winner
A prize pool over 1 million dollars for open solutions
Free API credits with no cash award
answer: A prize pool over 1 million dollars for open solutions
explanation: Chollet and Mike Knoop launched the ARC Prize with a seven-figure pool rewarding open solutions that beat tough score thresholds. A travel-grant-sized prize would not move frontier teams. The contest required public code so every winning approach taught the field something.

text: The 2022 BIG-bench suite plays on the name of which earlier test of machine intelligence?
options: The Loebner Prize finals
The Winograd Schema Challenge
The Elo chess rating
Turing's Imitation Game
answer: Turing's Imitation Game
explanation: BIG-bench stands for Beyond the Imitation Game, signaling hundreds of tasks meant to probe abilities Turing's conversational test misses. The Winograd Schema is a different commonsense test sometimes folded into SuperGLUE. The full name is the sticky clue to its crowd-sourced, everything-including-wordplay design.

text: The 2022 BIG-bench Hard subset was assembled to fix what problem with the full BIG-bench?
options: Most BIG-bench tasks were already too easy for large models
The full suite ran only on vision models
The full suite required live human voters
The full suite tested only Python code
answer: Most BIG-bench tasks were already too easy for large models
explanation: BIG-bench Hard kept the roughly two dozen tasks where the best models still trailed average human raters, filtering out tasks models had already cleared. Live human voting describes Chatbot Arena, not a static suite. The hard slice became the standard reasoning report because the full 200-task average had stopped separating models.

text: The 2018 GLUE benchmark bundled nine English tasks to measure what?
options: Speech-to-text transcription accuracy
General language understanding across entailment, sentiment and similarity
Image captioning quality
Robotic arm control success
answer: General language understanding across entailment, sentiment and similarity
explanation: GLUE averages entailment, sentiment, paraphrase and related sentence tasks into one general-understanding score. Speech transcription is a wholly audio problem with different metrics. GLUE's single-number design worked until BERT beat its human baseline within a year.

text: Researchers released SuperGLUE in 2019 largely because of what had happened to GLUE?
options: Its test server had been permanently deleted
Its tasks had been shown to contain no English
Models such as BERT had passed its human baseline within a year
Courts had banned its use for commercial models
answer: Models such as BERT had passed its human baseline within a year
explanation: BERT and its successors cleared GLUE's headroom almost immediately, so SuperGLUE assembled harder tasks with trickier reasoning and coreference. A deleted test server would be an infrastructure mishap, not a reason to design harder tasks. SuperGLUE itself then saturated the same way, the classic benchmark lifecycle.

text: The 2018 SQuAD 2.0 update added what kind of question that SQuAD 1.1 lacked?
options: Questions written in twelve new languages
Spoken questions read aloud by actors
Questions about images instead of text
Questions with no answer in the passage
answer: Questions with no answer in the passage
explanation: SQuAD 2.0 added 50,000 plausible-but-unanswerable questions so models must abstain instead of guessing a span. Multilingual questions came later with XQuAD and MLQA, not this update. The abstention requirement is why SQuAD 2.0 scores ran well below the original.

text: The 2016 SQuAD reading-comprehension dataset was released by which university group?
options: The MIT CSAIL language group
The Stanford NLP group
The Oxford VGG vision group
The Toronto Vector Institute team
answer: The Stanford NLP group
explanation: Pranav Rajpurkar and colleagues at Stanford released SQuAD with Wikipedia passages and crowd-written span answers. The Oxford VGG group is a vision lab known for image models, not reading comprehension. Stanford's 2016 release kicked off the BERT-era question-answering boom.

text: The 2022 HELM holistic evaluation framework came from which Stanford center?
options: The Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM)
The Stanford Linear Accelerator Center
The Hoover Institution economics group
The Stanford Medical School genetics lab
answer: The Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM)
explanation: Percy Liang's CRFM built HELM to evaluate models across many scenarios and metrics instead of one headline number. The Linear Accelerator Center is a physics facility, not a language-model lab. CRFM's living-benchmark design keeps adding scenarios as older ones saturate.

source.label: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models on arXiv

answerAliases: Center for Research on Foundation Models

text: The 2023 MT-Bench benchmark from UC Berkeley tests chat assistants with how many multi-turn questions?
options: 8 questions
24 questions
80 questions across 8 categories
8,000 questions
answer: 80 questions across 8 categories
explanation: MT-Bench uses 80 two-turn questions spanning writing, math, coding and reasoning, scored by a strong judge model. The 8,000-question distractor confuses it with a bulk static suite. The small curated size is deliberate: every answer gets judged, so quality matters more than quantity.

source.label: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench on arXiv

text: In the 2023 MT-Bench design, what makes the second turn of each item hard?
options: It switches to a completely unrelated language
It is a follow-up that depends on the model's own first answer
It asks the model to output only random numbers
It requires uploading an image file
answer: It is a follow-up that depends on the model's own first answer
explanation: Each MT-Bench item is two turns where the follow-up refers back, testing whether the assistant tracks conversation state and stays consistent. A language switch would test translation, not dialogue. The follow-up design is why single-turn tests miss failures that MT-Bench catches.

source.label: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench on arXiv

text: The 2025 Humanity's Last Exam benchmark collected roughly how many expert questions?
options: About 300 questions
About 800 questions
About 30,000 questions
About 3,000 questions across a hundred subjects
answer: About 3,000 questions across a hundred subjects
explanation: Humanity's Last Exam gathered around three thousand hard closed-ended questions across mathematics, science and humanities. Thirty thousand would be a bulk web scrape, the opposite of its expert-crafted design. Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety filtered thousands of submissions down to that final set.

source.label: Humanity's Last Exam paper on arXiv

text: Humanity's Last Exam was launched in 2025 mainly to solve what problem?
options: Frontier models had saturated older tests such as MMLU and GPQA
Chat models had become too slow to evaluate
Open models refused to answer science questions
Training GPUs had become too cheap to meter
answer: Frontier models had saturated older tests such as MMLU and GPQA
explanation: MMLU and GPQA scores had climbed so high they no longer separated frontier systems, so HLE commissioned far harder expert questions with a low-ceiling target. Evaluation speed was never the bottleneck a new benchmark would fix. Its launch scores near zero showed the headroom was real.

source.label: Humanity's Last Exam paper on arXiv

text: Epoch AI's 2024 FrontierMath benchmark keeps its math problems unpublished primarily to prevent what?
options: Crowdworkers solving them too cheaply
Journals publishing the solutions first
Models memorizing the problems during web-scale training
Volunteers translating them into other languages
answer: Models memorizing the problems during web-scale training
explanation: FrontierMath commissions brand-new problems and withholds them so they cannot leak into training scrapes and inflate scores. Cheap crowdworker solutions would be a cost issue, not a validity one. The secrecy is the whole defense against the contamination that killed older math tests.

text: In Epoch AI's 2024 FrontierMath design, what are the Tier 4 problems meant to be?
options: Quick warm-up arithmetic for calibration
Exceptionally hard problems taking expert mathematicians hours or days
Multiple-choice trivia about famous mathematicians
Python debugging tasks with no math
answer: Exceptionally hard problems taking expert mathematicians hours or days
explanation: Tier 4 holds closed research-level problems that stump working mathematicians for days, guarding headroom long after easier tiers fall. Warm-up arithmetic would defeat a benchmark built for the frontier. The tiered design lets scores climb gradually instead of jumping from zero to saturated.

text: A 2023 SWE-bench task counts as solved only when the model's patch passes which tests?
options: Only a single style check for code formatting
Only a human vote on code elegance
Only the model's own self-generated tests
The previously failing tests plus the previously passing regression tests
answer: The previously failing tests plus the previously passing regression tests
explanation: SWE-bench requires the FAIL_TO_PASS tests to flip to passing while the PASS_TO_PASS set stays green, proving the fix works without breaking anything. A style check alone says nothing about correctness. The two-sided gate is why SWE-bench scores run far below HumanEval function-writing scores.

text: The 2023 SWE-bench dataset built its 2,294 tasks from what raw material?
options: Real GitHub issues and pull requests from popular Python repositories
Synthetic puzzles written by a language model
End-of-chapter exercises from programming textbooks
Anonymized chatbot conversation logs
answer: Real GitHub issues and pull requests from popular Python repositories
explanation: Each SWE-bench task pairs a genuine repository issue with the merged pull request that fixed it, plus its test patch. Synthetic puzzles would miss the messy cross-file context of real codebases. The Princeton team mined a dozen popular Python projects for the original 2,294 instances.

text: The 2023 GPQA benchmark calls its questions Google-proof to mean what?
options: The questions cannot be viewed in a web browser
Google paid to keep the questions offline forever
Domain experts given web access still answer many of them incorrectly
Only Google employees are allowed to answer them
answer: Domain experts given web access still answer many of them incorrectly
explanation: GPQA filtered for questions that PhDs outside their specialty get wrong even with unrestricted search, hence Google-proof. An unviewable web page would make evaluation impossible rather than hard. The validation used paid expert annotators, which is why the surviving 448 Diamond questions stay brutal.

text: The 2023 GPQA graduate-level benchmark was led by researchers including David Rein from which kind of team?
options: An OpenAI internal red-team working alone
A New York University team working with Anthropic researchers
A Google DeepMind robotics group working alone
A Meta advertising ranking team working alone
answer: A New York University team working with Anthropic researchers
explanation: Rein and colleagues at NYU built GPQA with Anthropic collaborators after finding frontier models had cleared existing science tests. A robotics group would be an odd home for graduate biology and chemistry questions. The academic-lab plus frontier-lab pairing matched the goal of a ceiling-setting science test.

text: Greg Kamradt's 2023 needle-in-a-haystack test finds models suffer most when the hidden fact is placed where?
options: Buried in the middle of the long context
Placed as the very first sentence
Placed as the very last sentence
Repeated in every paragraph
answer: Buried in the middle of the long context
explanation: Recall forms a U-shape: facts at the start and end are retrieved well while middle-depth facts are lost, the famous lost-in-the-middle effect. First-sentence placement is the easy case the test uses as a control. The depth heatmap is the sticky visual every long-context launch still gets judged against.

source.label: Needle In A Haystack test by Greg Kamradt

text: Hugh Loebner's 1990 Loebner Prize competition implemented which format?
options: A chess tournament between programs and grandmasters
A mathematics olympiad graded by professors
A robot obstacle course judged on speed
Panels of judges holding short text conversations with programs and humans
answer: Panels of judges holding short text conversations with programs and humans
explanation: Loebner staged a restricted Turing test: judges chatted in text with hidden humans and programs, then ranked who seemed most human. A chess tournament would test search, not conversation. The restricted format with set topics is why AI researchers dismissed wins by chatbots such as A.L.I.C.E. as clever evasion.

text: Arpad Elo, whose rating system was adopted by the US Chess Federation in 1960, was what by profession?
options: A professional tennis champion
A television game-show host
A Hungarian-American physics professor
A serving US senator
answer: A Hungarian-American physics professor
explanation: Elo was a Hungarian-American physics professor and strong chess master who devised statistically principled ratings from win probabilities. A tennis champion would point at ranking points, a different system entirely. FIDE adopted his method in 1970, and Chatbot Arena borrows it for pairwise model votes.

text: The 2024 MMLU-Pro benchmark hardened MMLU in two ways. What changed?
options: It translated every question into twelve new languages
It replaced text with spoken questions read by actors
It cut the subject count down to a single topic
It expanded options from four to ten and filtered out the questions models found easy
answer: It expanded options from four to ten and filtered out the questions models found easy
explanation: MMLU-Pro grew the options to ten, which crushes lucky guessing, and pruned the questions models already aced. Translation into new languages is a different project, not this harder successor, which kept the broad subject spread.

text: The 2022 MGSM benchmark extends GSM8K to other languages. What does it contain?
options: The same grade-school problems translated into ten languages, a few hundred per language
Ten thousand new calculus problems in English only
Spoken math dictations recorded by voice actors
University physics exams with no worked solutions
answer: The same grade-school problems translated into ten languages, a few hundred per language
explanation: MGSM translates the same grade-school problems into ten languages so reasoning can be compared across tongues. English-only calculus would test harder math, not multilinguality, which is the benchmark's entire point.

text: The 2021 MBPP benchmark tests code generation with what kind of problems?
options: Fixing real bugs in decade-old operating-system kernels
Designing new programming languages from scratch
Around a thousand short Python tasks solvable by entry-level programmers
Proving theorems in formal math notation
answer: Around a thousand short Python tasks solvable by entry-level programmers
explanation: MBPP holds around a thousand short Python tasks an entry-level programmer could solve, each with tests. Kernel bugs belong to SWE-bench's world of real repositories, not this fundamentals check.

text: The 2022 DS-1000 benchmark targets data-science code with realistic problems from which libraries?
options: Fifty puzzles using only the standard library
A thousand problems drawn from libraries such as NumPy, pandas and PyTorch
Ten million auto-generated one-liners with no tests
A hundred essay questions about statistics history
answer: A thousand problems drawn from libraries such as NumPy, pandas and PyTorch
explanation: A thousand StackOverflow-style problems across pandas, NumPy and PyTorch test whether models write the glue code data scientists actually run. Essay questions about history would test trivia, not the ability to produce runnable analysis code.

text: The 2017 SciQ benchmark tests science exam knowledge. What form do its questions take?
options: Open-ended lab reports graded by teachers
Robot arm control tasks in a simulator
Spoken questions answered aloud by actors
Thirteen thousand multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry and biology
answer: Thirteen thousand multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry and biology
explanation: SciQ packages thirteen thousand crowd-written science questions as four-way multiple choice with supporting passages. Lab reports would need human graders, which is why the benchmark sticks to a format machines can score.

text: The 2019 WinoGrande benchmark scaled up the Winograd Schema Challenge. What makes its items hard?
options: Twin sentences differing by one word that flips which noun a pronoun refers to
Paragraphs of pure random characters with no meaning
Questions that require uploading an image file
Math proofs that take experts hours or days
answer: Twin sentences differing by one word that flips which noun a pronoun refers to
explanation: Each item is a pair of sentences identical except for a trigger word that flips the pronoun's referent, forcing genuine commonsense over statistics. Random characters would test nothing at all, since there is no meaning to resolve.

text: The 2019 PIQA benchmark tests physical commonsense. What does each item ask?
options: The exact melting point of an obscure alloy
A formal proof of a geometry theorem
Which of two solutions better achieves an everyday physical goal, like separating egg whites
The publication year of a famous physics paper
answer: Which of two solutions better achieves an everyday physical goal, like separating egg whites
explanation: PIQA asks which of two everyday fixes works, like using a fork versus a spoon to separate egg whites, probing physical intuition no textbook states outright. Melting points are lookup facts, the opposite of the reasoning it targets.

text: The 2016 Story Cloze Test gives a model four sentences of a story and asks what?
options: The author's birthplace and nationality
Which of two candidate endings correctly finishes the story
How many words appear in each sentence
A translation of the story into another language
answer: Which of two candidate endings correctly finishes the story
explanation: Given four context sentences, the model must pick the sensible fifth from two candidates, which demands tracking characters' goals rather than word overlap. Counting words is a tokenization chore that reveals nothing about story understanding.

source.label: Story Cloze Test paper on arXiv

text: The 2018 MultiRC benchmark differs from SQuAD-style tests in what way?
options: Its questions need reasoning across several sentences, and more than one answer option can be correct
It asks models to output only random numbers
It tests vision models on labeled images
It ranks chatbots through live human votes
answer: Its questions need reasoning across several sentences, and more than one answer option can be correct
explanation: MultiRC questions hinge on several sentences scattered through a paragraph, and crucially several options may be right, so partial credit matters. Single-span SQuAD questions have exactly one answer, which is the format MultiRC deliberately outgrew.

text: The 2019 DROP benchmark punishes models that only match text spans. What must models do instead?
options: Extracting exact answer spans quoted from the passage
Translating passages into twelve new languages
Retrieving evidence and labeling claims supported or refuted
Perform discrete operations like counting, sorting and arithmetic over the passage
answer: Perform discrete operations like counting, sorting and arithmetic over the passage
explanation: DROP passages require counting, sorting, adding and comparing numbers found in text, so span-matching models collapse on it. Translation would test language transfer, not the discrete reasoning the benchmark was built to demand.

text: The 2019 CoQA benchmark tests conversational question answering. How is it structured?
options: Single questions about isolated trivia facts
Chess puzzles with one forced mate
Free-form dialogue turns where later questions depend on the conversation history
Python functions to complete from docstrings
answer: Free-form dialogue turns where later questions depend on the conversation history
explanation: CoQA chains free-form questions in a conversation, so later ones lean on pronouns and history the model must track. Isolated trivia would need no memory at all, which is precisely the skill CoQA adds over SQuAD.

text: The 2017 TriviaQA benchmark is distinctive among reading tests for what?
options: Questions written by models with no human review
Trivia questions paired with independently gathered evidence documents that share little wording with the questions
Questions about images instead of text
A fixed set of eight questions reused every year
answer: Trivia questions paired with independently gathered evidence documents that share little wording with the questions
explanation: TriviaQA pairs enthusiast-written trivia with evidence documents gathered independently of the questions, so wording rarely overlaps and models must genuinely comprehend. Image questions belong to visual benchmarks like VQA, a different modality entirely.

text: The 2018 FEVER benchmark tests fact verification. What must a model do for each claim?
options: Retrieve Wikipedia evidence and label the claim supported, refuted or not enough info
Write a poem about the claim's subject
Generate a photorealistic image of the event
Predict the claim's stock-market impact
answer: Retrieve Wikipedia evidence and label the claim supported, refuted or not enough info
explanation: FEVER requires retrieving the right Wikipedia sentences and then judging each claim supported, refuted or undecidable from them. Writing poetry about the subject would dodge both retrieval and judgment, the benchmark's two halves.

text: The 2018 ARC benchmark from the Allen Institute tests grade-school science, split into Easy and Challenge sets. What defines the Challenge set?
options: Questions written in twelve new languages
Spoken questions read aloud by actors
Questions that both retrieval and word-co-occurrence baselines answer incorrectly
Questions with no correct answer at all
answer: Questions that both retrieval and word-co-occurrence baselines answer incorrectly
explanation: The Challenge set keeps only the science questions that simple retrieval and co-occurrence systems miss, so it measures reasoning rather than search. Note the name clash: unlike ARC-AGI's grid puzzles, this ARC is grade-school science with an Easy sibling set.

text: The 2022 CodeContests benchmark from DeepMind collects competitive-programming problems. What makes them harder than HumanEval-style tasks?
options: They must be solved without writing any code
They test only code formatting style
They are single-line completions with no tests
They demand full programs that parse input, handle edge cases and pass hidden tests under limits
answer: They demand full programs that parse input, handle edge cases and pass hidden tests under limits
explanation: CodeContests problems come from real competitions, demanding full programs with parsing, edge cases and efficiency, far beyond completing a docstring function. Style-only grading would ignore whether the code runs, which is the whole point of hidden tests.
